title: DataFrames transformations and grouped summaries
outcome: Transform a typed table and compute grouped summaries while preserving names, missingness and row counts.
key_terms: A table from DataFrames.jl whose named columns are vectors that may each have a different element type.
Choosing output columns explicitly, where `df[!, :x]` shares the stored vector and `df[:, :x]` returns a copy.
A wrapper that makes a `select` or `transform` function receive one row's values at a time instead of whole columns.
A function that splits a data frame by key columns, usually followed by `combine` to produce one row per group.
Recording row counts before and after each filter or reshaping step so every removed or duplicated row is explained.
approach: Track three things through every DataFrames step: column names, row counts and storage sharing. `select` with `ByRow` and `copycols = true` builds a new named column, `input[!, :score]` returns the stored column while `input[:, :score]` copies it, and grouped summaries pair `observed_mean` with row and observed counts.

exercises.title: Name the derived field
exercises.task: Scale the score column by 10 using ByRow.
exercises.expected: The output column contains 1, 2 and 3 under the explicit name `scaled`.
exercises.answer: Names and shape are part of the resulting schema.
exercises.why: `:score => ByRow(x -> x / 10) => :scaled` applies the function to each of 10, 20 and 30 and names the result `scaled`.
exercises.wrong: Writing `:score => (x -> x / 10)` without a name produces an automatic column name that downstream code has to guess.

exercises.title: Observe a shared column
exercises.hint: The indexing operation can return the stored column.
exercises.answer: A caller must request a copy when independent storage is required.
exercises.why: `input[!, :score]` returns the column object stored in the table, so `alias[1] = 99` makes `input.score[1]` equal 99.
exercises.wrong: Treating `!` as a harmless spelling of `:` assumes a copy, which leads to accidental edits of the source table.
exercises.verify: Example A asserts `input.score[1] == 99` after the alias write.

exercises.title: Retain a column snapshot
exercises.task: Copy the column before later source mutation.
exercises.answer: A snapshot is useful for comparison and provenance when future mutation is possible.
exercises.why: `input[:, :score]` copies the column, so the snapshot still holds 10 after the alias write.
exercises.wrong: Checking only that the snapshot equals the column at creation time cannot reveal sharing; the test must mutate the source afterward.
exercises.verify: Example A asserts `snapshot[1] == 10`; the reference checks `select(...; copycols = true).id !== input.id`.

exercises.title: Report group coverage
exercises.task: Summarize the group containing one missing score.
exercises.expected: It reports 2 rows, 1 observed score and mean 1.
exercises.hint: A mean alone hides the denominator.
exercises.answer: Row accounting remains necessary after grouping.
exercises.why: Group a has scores 1 and missing, so `nrow` is 2, the observed count is 1 and `observed_mean` gives 1.0.
exercises.wrong: Reporting only `mean_score` makes group a look as well supported as group b, which has two observed scores.

exercises.title: Handle an all-missing group
exercises.task: Apply observed_mean to only missing values.
exercises.hint: An empty observed set needs a stated policy.
exercises.answer: A fabricated zero could change later model or business decisions.
exercises.why: With every score missing, the observed set is empty and `observed_mean` returns `missing` rather than a number.
exercises.wrong: Using `mean(skipmissing(x))` directly throws on the empty iterator or, with a default, invents a zero.

exercises.title: Interpret a mean of means
exercises.task: Average the two group means with and without count weights.
exercises.answer: Group-level and row-level summaries represent different populations.
exercises.why: The unweighted mean of group means 1.0 and 4.0 is 2.5; weighting by observed counts 1 and 2 gives (1 + 8) / 3 = 3.0.
exercises.wrong: Averaging group means without weights and calling it the overall mean treats one observation in group a like two in group b.
exercises.verify: Compute both values from the summary table and compare 3.0 with `mean([1, 3, 5])`, the row-level observed mean.

checks_note: `observed_mean([missing])` returns missing because no observed value remains. The `DataFrame` lines confirm that `transform` returns a new table with a `square` column of `[4, 16]` while the input keeps only `id` and `x` with two rows. The final line checks that `select` with `copycols = true` gives a fresh `id` vector, so writing to the result cannot alter `input`.
